title: Install with a recovery plan
summary: Prepare, deploy, and verify an operating system.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: An operating system installation can replace an existing environment or upgrade it in place. A clean install creates a fresh environment and may erase existing data, while an upgrade aims to retain supported applications and settings. Neither option removes the need for a verified backup. Check hardware requirements, driver availability, application compatibility, licensing, and the intended installation source before starting. A recovery plan must be usable even if the new operating system fails to boot.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: Boot media can be local, removable, or network-based. Match the firmware’s supported boot mode and partitioning requirements to the operating system; modern UEFI deployments commonly use GPT. An image deployment can standardize many machines, but the image still needs appropriate drivers, updates, and organization-specific configuration. After installation, validate network access, device functionality, updates, security configuration, and required applications. Confirm that the user can perform their actual work, then document the outcome and preserve the agreed recovery path until the change is accepted.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
